summary:
Samara Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned since 2023, same-sex marriage is prohibited, and no discrimination protection is available to transgender people. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records these as the operative national conditions, along with 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

That note assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of their sexual orientation, while trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. A trans visitor to Samara Oblast falls within the second category. The note records no division-specific facts for Samara Oblast.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions by that date for alleged participation in the designated International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols: 98 administrative and 3 criminal. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024 onward, and three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years' imprisonment. Repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years. These are national-level figures and they apply within Samara Oblast.

At the national level, foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and the propaganda statute reaches expression that "justifies" gender transition. The Supreme Court's designation of the International LGBT Movement as extremist, made in January 2024, was followed within 48 hours by raids on LGBTQ+ venues in Moscow, in which about 100 patrons at one bar were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws grew eighteenfold over the preceding decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years.

Deaths in custody have been recorded in extremism-related proceedings. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

The US State Department advises Level 4, Do Not Travel for Russia, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Residents of Samara Oblast face the same national regime as visitors on the legal side: gender-affirming care and legal gender change are prohibited, and there is no statutory discrimination protection. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, with one St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no division-specific reporting for Samara Oblast: no documented arrests, raids, local ordinances or enforcement actions particular to this oblast are sourced here. All findings above rest on the national framework and national-level enforcement data, which the Home Office note confirms applies without division-specific qualification.

The 101 convictions figure is a national cumulative total to 30 June 2025 and is not broken down by region, so the share attributable to Samara Oblast is unresolved. Likewise the 139-person impact figure for 2022 to 2024 is not disaggregated by oblast.
